findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Normal sinus rhythm. Normal axis and intervals. No acute ST-T changes.
Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a posterior-predominant cortical profile. Visuospatial and visuoperceptual abilities are severely impaired: Judgment of Line Orientation 12/30, Hooper Visual Organization 15.4/30, Rey Complex Figure Copy 17/36 (the delayed recall of 9/36 is limited by the poor copy). Processing speed (WAIS-IV PSI 75) and perceptual reasoning (PRI 76) are in the borderline range. Set-shifting is impaired (Trail Making B, 132 seconds). Episodic verbal memory (CVLT-3 Long Delay z = -0.5), naming and verbal comprehension (VCI 99) are relatively preserved. Profile is consistent with a posterior cortical syndrome with visuospatial predominance.

findings.value: Fixation losses frequent; target detection slowed

output.impression: Full peripheral visual fields in both eyes with normal acuity and colour vision; frequent fixation losses reduce reliability. No field defect explaining the reading difficulty.
Normal peripapillary retinal nerve fibre layer and macular thickness in both eyes.

findings.signal: cortical_to_cerebellar_ratio: Elevated (SUVR 1.52, positive threshold >1.11); regional_pattern: Diffuse cortical amyloid deposition with highest uptake in precuneus, posterior cingulate, and lateral parietal cortex

output.impression: POSITIVE amyloid PET: moderate to frequent cortical amyloid neuritic plaque density, highest in precuneus, posterior cingulate and lateral parietal cortex. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.interpretation: Opening pressure 15 cmH2O. WBC 1 cell/uL. Protein 38 mg/dL. Glucose 66 mg/dL (CSF/serum ratio 0.58). Abeta42/40 ratio 0.042, decreased (Abeta42 412 pg/mL, Abeta40 9800 pg/mL). p-tau181 91 pg/mL and total tau 640 pg/mL, elevated. Pattern: decreased Abeta42/40 with elevated p-tau and total tau, the Alzheimer biomarker pattern. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.signal: pattern: Marked hypometabolism in bilateral parieto-occipital regions, right > left, extending into posterior temporal cortex; parietal_SUVr: 0.78 (normal >0.95); occipital_SUVr: 0.82 (normal >0.95); frontal_SUVr: 0.96 (normal); medial_temporal_SUVr: 0.97 (normal)

output.impression: Posterior-predominant hypometabolism of bilateral parieto-occipital cortex, right greater than left, extending into posterior temporal cortex, with relative sparing of frontal and medial temporal regions. Clinical correlation recommended.

alternatives: Rivastigmine transdermal patch 4.6 mg/24 h: may reduce gastrointestinal effects.
Galantamine ER 8 mg daily: alternative cholinesterase inhibitor.
interactions: Donepezil + Amlodipine: no clinically significant interaction; amlodipine does not slow the heart rate.
Donepezil + Aspirin: cholinesterase inhibitors increase gastric acid secretion; with aspirin, monitor for dyspepsia and gastrointestinal bleeding.
Donepezil + Metformin, Rosuvastatin, Vitamin D3: no clinically significant interaction.
warnings: Vagotonic effect: bradycardia, heart block and syncope can occur; baseline pulse 78 bpm and no rate-slowing medicine on the list. Check pulse at each dose increase.
Nausea, diarrhoea, anorexia and weight loss are common at initiation; start at 5 mg at night and increase to 10 mg after 4 to 6 weeks if tolerated.
Anticholinergic medicines oppose the effect of cholinesterase inhibitors; avoid combining.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Visuospatial-predominant impairment (simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, oculomotor apraxia, left extinction, reading errors) with relatively spared recall, husband-confirmed decline, and loss of instrumental independence (driving stopped, work duties removed)
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive assessment with informant history: a validated bedside instrument with the per-domain breakdown, tests of visuospatial and visuoperceptual function (Balint signs), the effect of cueing on recall, and an explicit account of which instrumental activities have been lost
action_criteria.rationale: Her complaints are visual, so bedside testing must show the cortical visuospatial syndrome and the preserved memory that define posterior cortical atrophy, and stage its functional impact [PCA_consensus_2017].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Severe visuospatial and visuoperceptual impairment (line orientation, visual organisation, figure copy) with relatively preserved verbal memory, naming and comprehension
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile and establish a baseline for tracking
action_criteria.rationale: Formal testing quantifies the visuospatial deficits against preserved verbal memory and language, the profile that separates posterior cortical atrophy from amnestic Alzheimer disease, and sets a baseline [PCA_consensus_2017].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TSH, B12, folate, syphilis and HIV serology normal; HbA1c 6.4%
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Reversible metabolic, endocrine and infectious contributors are excluded before a neurodegenerative cause is assigned [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Posterior-predominant parieto-occipital cortical atrophy with relative sparing of medial temporal structures
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to show the pattern of atrophy and exclude an occipitoparietal mass, infarct or prion disease
action_criteria.rationale: Parieto-occipital atrophy with spared hippocampi supports posterior cortical atrophy, and MRI excludes a structural lesion or cortical diffusion restriction that would explain the visual syndrome [PCA_consensus_2017].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Full visual fields with normal acuity and colour vision, or a normal retinal nerve fibre layer on OCT: no ocular or optic nerve cause for the reading difficulty
action_criteria.label: Obtain formal visual fields or optical coherence tomography to exclude an ocular or optic nerve cause
action_criteria.rationale: Patients with posterior cortical atrophy often present to eye services first; a normal ophthalmic examination shows the deficit is cortical [PCA_consensus_2017].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity: a positive amyloid PET with posterior-predominant cortical binding, or a decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio with raised p-tau181 and total tau
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and it is needed when the diagnosis remains uncertain after the clinical, neuropsychological and MRI assessment or when disease-modifying treatment is being considered [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral parieto-occipital and posterior cingulate hypometabolism with relative sparing of frontal cortex
action_criteria.label: Consider FDG-PET after the clinical assessment, labs and MRI if the cause of the posterior cortical syndrome remains uncertain
action_criteria.rationale: Parieto-occipital hypometabolism with frontal sparing supports Alzheimer-type posterior cortical atrophy over corticobasal degeneration or Lewy body disease when MRI is not conclusive [Foster_2007].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Donepezil can be started: no significant interaction with her medicines, gastrointestinal caution with aspirin, pulse check for bradycardia
action_criteria.label: After the diagnosis is staged and disclosed, check donepezil against her current medicines before starting it
action_criteria.rationale: A post-diagnostic safety step before the cholinesterase inhibitor that mild Alzheimer dementia supports [NICE_NG97].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the reading and visuospatial difficulties to her mild cataracts or offer cataract surgery or new spectacles as the solution; acuity of 20/25 and full fields point to a cortical cause [PCA_consensus_2017].
Do not start memantine at the mild dementia stage; it is indicated for moderate or severe Alzheimer disease or when cholinesterase inhibitors are not tolerated [NICE_NG97].
required_recommendations: Disclose posterior cortical atrophy due to Alzheimer disease to the patient and her husband, explaining that the visual problems arise in the brain and not the eyes, and discuss prognosis, advance directives and durable power of attorney [PCA_consensus_2017].
Refer for ophthalmology and low-vision assessment to exclude an ocular cause and to support reading and mobility [PCA_consensus_2017].

Offer a trial of a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine) for mild Alzheimer dementia after checking pulse, conduction history and current medicines (pulse 78 bpm, no rate-slowing medicine) [NICE_NG97].

Address work and safety: she should not resume driving and the licensing authority should be informed per local rules; support an occupational health review of her employment and financial and legal planning; refer to occupational therapy for visuospatial strategies at home [PCA_consensus_2017].

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardiac symptom or syncope to justify it in this case
Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
Head CT adds little when MRI is available; MRI is the preferred structural modality for dementia workup

accepted: Posterior cortical atrophy (Benson syndrome), early-onset Alzheimer's disease pathology

differential.key_features: Apraxia, cortical sensory loss (impaired graphesthesia, left astereognosis) and sequencing errors overlap with corticobasal syndrome, but there is no asymmetric rigidity, dystonia, myoclonus or alien limb, and the posterior-predominant atrophy and hypometabolism with amyloid positivity point to Alzheimer pathology
Visuoperceptual deficits overlap, but there are no visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM sleep behavior disorder or fluctuations
Excluded by structural MRI showing atrophy without a mass, infarct or microbleeds
The Heidenhain variant progresses over weeks; this course has been gradual over eighteen months without myoclonus, and MRI shows no cortical diffusion restriction
Corrected acuity 20/25, normal colour vision, full visual fields and normal OCT; the deficits are of higher-order visual processing (Balint signs, simultanagnosia, alexia)
Fazekas 2 white matter disease with hypertension and diabetes, but no infarct or lacune; a posterior cortical visuospatial syndrome with parieto-occipital cortical atrophy is not a vascular pattern

key_clinical_evidence: In posterior cortical atrophy the presenting deficits are visuospatial and visuoperceptual with relatively preserved memory; patients often see an optometrist first, and Alzheimer pathology is the most common cause [PCA_consensus_2017].

Normal hippocampal volumes do not exclude Alzheimer disease: atypical variants show atrophy and hypometabolism where the clinical deficits are, here parieto-occipital [PCA_consensus_2017] [Foster_2007].

Simultanagnosia, optic ataxia and oculomotor apraxia (Balint syndrome) are tested at the bedside and localise to the dorsal visual stream; they explain misreaching, misjudged distances and reading failure despite normal acuity.
White matter hyperintensities in a patient with vascular risk factors should not divert a posterior cortical syndrome with focal cortical atrophy toward a vascular diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The cataracts are mild and stable with corrected acuity 20/25; they do not cause simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, left extinction or environmental disorientation, which are cortical signs
red_herrings.data_point: Mild bilateral cataracts, stable on last ophthalmology exam 6 months ago
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the reading and visual difficulties to an ocular cause and stop the cognitive work-up

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect
Amyloid biomarkers are interpreted against an established clinical syndrome; they are not a screening test.
The cholinesterase-inhibitor safety check follows the staging of the syndrome as dementia.

findings.result: Alert and oriented to person, place, date, and situation.
MMSE 26/30, losing points on serial sevens (2 errors), pentagon copy and the reading item (misread the written command).

MoCA 23/30 with particular difficulty on visuospatial/executive tasks (cube copy distorted, clock drawing with numbers clustered to the right side, trail-making B errors). Delayed recall 4/5, the fifth word retrieved with a categorical cue.

Simultanagnosia on the Cookie Theft picture (describes single elements, cannot report the whole scene); optic ataxia, misreaching for targets in the peripheral fields, worse on the left; mild oculomotor apraxia with hypometric voluntary saccades; left visual extinction on double simultaneous stimulation (3 of 5 trials); letter substitution errors when reading.

Her husband reports eighteen months of progressive difficulty reading blueprints and text, misjudging distances, knocking over objects, walking into door frames on the left, and getting lost in a familiar shopping mall. Memory for recent conversations and events remains good.

She stopped driving six months ago after sideswiping a parked car, following several near-misses, and has been moved to non-design duties at work because of errors in spatial layout. She still manages her medicines, bills and social calendar.

clinical_assessment.impression: MMSE 26/30 and MoCA 23/30, with impairment in visuospatial and visuoconstructive items, serial subtraction and reading, and relatively spared memory (delayed recall 4/5, the fifth word retrieved with a cue). Simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, mild oculomotor apraxia and left visual extinction are present. Her husband reports eighteen months of decline in reading, spatial judgement and navigation, with preserved recall of recent events. Repeated driving incidents ended her driving and work errors have removed her from design duties: independence in instrumental activities is lost, consistent with mild dementia with a posterior cortical, visuospatial-predominant profile.

patient.history_present_illness: Dr. Yuki Nakamura is a 65-year-old right-handed architect who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by her husband, James, for evaluation of progressive difficulty with visual and spatial tasks over the past eighteen months. Her husband reports that the first noticeable change occurred approximately eighteen months ago when she began struggling to read architectural blueprints at work, a task she had performed with ease for over thirty years. She initially attributed this to worsening vision and saw her ophthalmologist, who noted only mild, stable bilateral cataracts insufficient to explain her symptoms. Her corrected visual acuity was measured at 20/25 bilaterally at that time. Over the following months, she developed increasing difficulty reading text, frequently losing her place on the page and misidentifying letters, which she described as the words seeming to 'jump around.' She has had multiple near-miss incidents while driving, primarily involving misjudging distances when parking or changing lanes, and she voluntarily stopped driving six months ago after sideswiping a parked car. At her architecture firm, colleagues noted she was making errors in spatial layout and proportion that were uncharacteristic of her meticulous work, and she has had difficulty using computer-aided design software that she previously used expertly; four months ago the firm moved her to non-design duties. She has become noticeably clumsy, frequently knocking over glasses and reaching past objects she is trying to grasp. Her husband notes she occasionally walks into door frames on her left side. She recently became lost in a shopping mall she has visited for over twenty years, unable to orient herself to find the exit. Remarkably, her memory for conversations and events remains quite good. She accurately recalled details of a family dinner from the previous weekend, including who attended and what was discussed. She continues to manage her medications, pay bills, and maintain her social calendar without difficulty. She remains articulate and engages warmly in conversation. There have been no personality changes, behavioral disturbances, hallucinations, or mood symptoms beyond understandable frustration with her visual difficulties. She denies headaches, seizures, tremor, weakness, numbness, or difficulty walking. Her husband has not observed any features suggestive of REM sleep behavior disorder. She has had no episodes of fluctuating alertness or confusion.

neurological_exam.additional: Optic ataxia noted on reaching tasks: patient misreaches for objects placed in peripheral visual fields, particularly on the left side. Difficulty with visually guided hand movements despite intact primary motor and sensory function. No paratonic rigidity. No myoclonus. No grasp reflex.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally. Heel-to-shin intact. Rapid alternating movements intact. However, patient demonstrates significant difficulty with sequential finger tapping tasks and reproducing hand sequences (Luria test).
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light. Extraocular movements full, no nystagmus. Visual fields full to confrontation testing with standard finger counting; however, simultaneous bilateral stimulation reveals left visual extinction on 3 of 5 trials. Face symmetric. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady, normal base and stride. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative. No parkinsonian features.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, date, and situation. MMSE 26/30, losing points on serial sevens (2 errors), pentagons copy (unable to reproduce interlocking pentagons accurately) and the reading item (misread the written command). Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) 23/30 with particular difficulty on visuospatial/executive tasks (cube copy distorted, clock drawing with misplaced numbers clustered to right side, trail-making B errors). Delayed recall 4/5 words (retrieved the 5th with categorical cue). Naming intact. Repetition intact. Verbal fluency mildly reduced (12 animals in 60 seconds). Reading: occasional letter substitution errors. Writing: intact for dictated sentences.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk and tone normal throughout all extremities. Strength 5/5 in all muscle groups. No pronator drift. No tremor, rigidity, or involuntary movements.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric in biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No frontal release signs.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact throughout. Proprioception intact at great toes bilaterally. Vibration mildly reduced at bilateral medial malleoli (attributed to diabetic neuropathy). Graphesthesia impaired in bilateral hands (unable to identify 3 of 6 numbers traced on palm). Stereognosis impaired in left hand (unable to identify key, correctly identified coin and paperclip).
